intro: On the exam's calculation question, a reader gives one point for the setup and one for the answer with its unit. This studio grades both, the way they do. Start with the unit chain: snap conversion factors onto a number and watch the units cancel until only the one you want is left. Then test yourself on every calculation type the exam uses, each scenario new every time.
howItWorks:
The setup box reads what you type as Bluebook would: numbers, + − × ÷ (type * and /), ^ for powers, brackets, and units after a number ((150 - 120) / 120 * 100, 5000 kWh * 0.9 kg CO2/kWh). It checks the value, the brackets around a difference before you divide, the × 100 for a percent, and that your units cancel to the answer's unit. It never uses eval.

The answer box takes the number (2.5 million, 2.5e6 and 2,500,000 all work) and its unit separately, so you see which point you earned. Feedback names the slip: forgot × 100, divided by the new value, the 10% rule applied once too often, the doubling time not added to the year, a factor of 1,000 from a prefix.

Every key comes from the same calculation recipes as the course's questions (ApEnvCalc), recomputed by a checker on 300 problems per scenario. Significant figures are not graded (the readers do not grade them); answers within 1% are right. Scenarios use invented numbers in realistic ranges.

contexts.lead: Rangers count the white-tailed deer in a state park every winter.
A town weighs the plastic its households put out for recycling each year, in metric tons.
A fishing fleet reports its yearly cod catch, in metric tons.
An observatory reports the yearly average CO₂ concentration in parts per million (ppm).
A city produces {q} metric tons of municipal solid waste a year, and {pct}% of it is paper and cardboard.
contexts.ask: how many metric tons of paper and cardboard the city produces each year.

contexts.ask: how many cubic meters are lost to evaporation each year.
